opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a really fundamental tradeoff there that people often don't appreciate enough. If you had truly unlimited computing resources, then AGI would be almost trivially simple in principle. You know, Marcus Hutter's AIXI, or Schmidhuber's Gödel machine: these show that with infinite or absurdly huge compute, you can write down a general intelligence in a few lines of math. You just search over all possible programs, weight them by simplicity, and pick the actions that maximize expected reward. That's general intelligence, in a sense, but it's completely useless in practice, because the compute required is way beyond anything the physical universe could provide.

So the real question is never "what's the simplest algorithm for general intelligence?" It's "what's the simplest algorithm for general intelligence *given these particular resource constraints*?" And as you tighten the constraints, the algorithm necessarily gets more complicated. You have to build in more specialized structure, more heuristics, more inductive biases tuned to the kinds of environments and problems the system is actually going to face.

The human brain is a great example. We're not maximally general intelligences at all. We're quite specialized for the sorts of things that mattered for survival on the savanna: social reasoning, spatial navigation, recognizing faces, language. And the brain is this messy hodgepodge of different subsystems that evolved to deal with those things efficiently given the metabolic budget of a few watts. That messiness is the price of efficiency.

Now, what's interesting about the current moment is that we have a lot more compute than we used to. And part of what you're seeing with deep learning and large language models is that when compute gets cheap enough, relatively simple algorithms, you know, gradient descent on big neural nets plus lots of data, start doing things that used to seem to require a lot of careful hand-engineered structure. Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" is basically this point. But I don't think that means you can just scale up a simple algorithm all the way to human-level AGI and beyond. The simple stuff gets you remarkably far on pattern recognition and on interpolating within the space of what's in the training data, but for the kind of creative generalization and self-reflective reasoning that real AGI needs, I think you still need more cognitive architecture: different kinds of learning and reasoning interacting synergistically, which is what we've been trying to do with OpenCog Hyperon.

So my view is that more compute lets you get away with a simpler design, but not a trivially simple one. There's a sweet spot, where you have enough compute that you don't have to hand-code everything, but you still have a reasonably rich architecture that lets different algorithms cooperate and help each other past their respective combinatorial explosions. And I think finding that sweet spot for the hardware we'll have over the next few years is really the crux of the engineering problem of AGI right now.

r001.rationale: It says that with unlimited or enormous compute, AGI could be specified in only a few lines of math.

r002.rationale: It names AIXI and the Gödel machine and describes searching over possible programs, weighting them by simplicity, and selecting actions by expected reward.

r003.rationale: It says resource limits can require specialized structure, but does not attribute much of modern AI systems’ complexity to working around those limits. It instead says more compute lets relatively simple deep learning methods work.

r004.rationale: It favors multiple learning and reasoning methods cooperating within an AGI architecture, but does not connect this to heterogeneous computing infrastructure.

r005.rationale: It contrasts resource-conditioned algorithm simplicity with the simple AIXI and Gödel machine formulations, but does not make data a condition of that simplicity distinction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a fairly deep relationship there, and it's one that people often don't think about carefully enough. If you had truly unlimited computing resources, then AGI is in a sense trivial. You could just do something like AIXI, Marcus Hutter's formalism, where you enumerate all possible programs, weight them by simplicity, and pick whichever one best predicts your reward history. That's a few lines of math. It's provably optimal in a certain sense, and it's also completely uncomputable. Or you take AIXI-tl, the time and length bounded version, which is computable but would take longer than the lifetime of the universe to do anything interesting.

So the simplicity of the algorithm is inversely related, in a rough way, to the amount of compute you're willing to throw at it. Once you constrain yourself to a realistic amount of computing power, whether that's a human brain, which is remarkably efficient energetically, or a big data center, then you can no longer rely on brute force search over program space. You have to build in prior knowledge, you have to build in specialized heuristics, you have to have multiple different kinds of memory and learning that are tuned to the kinds of regularities that exist in our particular universe. And that's where all the complexity in the human brain comes from, really. Evolution had very tight resource constraints and ended up with this incredibly messy, heterogeneous architecture because that was what worked given the hardware.

My own view, which is behind the OpenCog Hyperon work, is that we're in the middle ground. We have way more compute than we did twenty years ago, so some things that used to require clever engineering can now be done more by learning, as the deep learning community has shown. But we're nowhere near the regime where you can just do the simple, elegant, mathematically pure thing. So I think a realistic AGI design is going to have a kind of layered simplicity. There's a simple core, something like a probabilistic logic and an evolutionary learning process acting on a common knowledge representation, and then a lot of specialized machinery built around it to make it tractable. And as compute keeps growing, you can gradually strip away some of that specialized scaffolding and let the more general mechanisms take over more of the load. It's really the amount of compute that determines where you draw that line.

r001.rationale: It says that with truly unlimited computing resources, AGI is nearly trivial and could use a few-lines-of-math approach like AIXI.

r002.rationale: It describes AIXI as enumerating possible programs, weighting them by simplicity, and selecting the one that best predicts reward history.

r003.rationale: It links resource constraints to the need for specialized heuristics and heterogeneous architectures, and says those constraints make realistic AGI designs more complex.

r004.rationale: It discusses different compute settings and heterogeneous internal machinery, but does not connect heterogeneous computing infrastructure to a need for heterogeneous operation within the AGI.

r005.rationale: It contrasts AIXI’s mathematical simplicity with resource-constrained designs, but does not distinguish simplicity conditional on both infrastructure and data.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a tradeoff between the simplicity of the algorithm and the amount of computing power you need to make it do something useful. You can describe a very general approach quite simply: search through possible programs, see which ones explain your observations, and use those to choose actions. But the search space is enormous. The difficulty is making that work with finite resources.

So a lot of the complexity in an AGI architecture comes from trying to be efficient. You introduce particular representations, learning mechanisms, and ways of directing attention so the system doesn’t spend all its time exploring things that aren’t relevant. Those mechanisms make the design more complicated, but they can dramatically reduce the computation it needs.

As computing resources increase, you may be able to dispense with some of that machinery and use more general methods. But I wouldn’t assume that means the simplest possible algorithm becomes practical. There’s a very big gap between having more computing power and having enough to do an essentially unrestricted search.

r001.rationale: It says more computing may allow more general methods, but explicitly cautions that even much more power may not make the simplest possible algorithm practical.

r002.rationale: It describes a simple general approach that searches possible programs, evaluates which explain observations, and uses them to choose actions.

r003.rationale: It attributes much of AGI architecture complexity to making systems efficient under finite computational resources.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss heterogeneous computing infrastructure or argue that it favors heterogeneous operation within the AGI system.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish simplicity conditional on infrastructure and data from intuitive algorithmic simplicity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s a tradeoff between the simplicity of the algorithm and the amount of computing power you need to make it do something interesting. If you have essentially unlimited computing resources, you can write down quite simple approaches: search through possible programs, see which ones predict your observations, and use those predictions to choose actions. The difficulty is that the search becomes astronomically expensive.

If you want a system that learns and acts in the world with the resources we actually have, you need more structure. You need ways to generalize from limited experience, to direct attention, to reuse what you’ve learned rather than starting the search over every time. And that tends to make the architecture more complicated.

So a very simple mathematical description of general intelligence may be possible without giving us a practical recipe for building it. The interesting question is how much complexity we need to introduce to make intelligence computationally feasible. And we don’t really know the minimum there.

r001.rationale: It says essentially unlimited computing resources could make quite simple approaches useful for interesting behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes searching possible programs, but does not identify AIXI or the Gödel machine, or clearly attribute their simplicity to brute-force search.

r003.rationale: It links the added structure and architectural complexity needed by practical learning systems to limited computing resources.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss heterogeneous computing infrastructure or favoring heterogeneous operation within the AGI.

r005.rationale: It contrasts mathematical simplicity with a practical recipe, but does not distinguish simplicity conditional on infrastructure and data or invoke AIXI or the Gödel machine.
